interactions.summary: Jiang completes the Florentine example by tying Dante's exile to the black-white Guelph split and restating that the church's involvement in temporal politics corrupts its teaching.

A student reads Justinian's lines about earthly honor deflecting love from heaven, and Jiang glosses them as Dante's core free-will model: human beings choose whether to aim their energies at God or at power and material gain.
interactions.speaker_attribution: student reading with Jiang interpretive gloss

interactions.summary: The reading introduces Romeo as a righteous servant repaid with ingratitude, and Jiang turns him into a Dante-parallel whose exile and poverty prove that true wealth is heavenly reward rather than worldly success.
interactions.speaker_attribution: student reading with Jiang moral-political gloss

interactions.summary: Jiang pivots from canto six into the problem of why Jesus had to die, and a student offers the first answer: Christ sacrifices himself to prove his divinity to doubters.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang framing question and student answer

speaker_notes.note: These segments are quoted Dante read aloud by a student; Jiang's explanatory voice enters in segments 0299, 0302, and 0303.

claims.claim: Jiang says the black Guelph victory over the white Guelphs is the immediate political event that exiles Dante.
Jiang says Dante reads that whole struggle as a corruption of church teaching, because the church should not fight over temporal power or the legacy of Rome.
Jiang presents free will as the central Divine Comedy principle that determines whether human energy moves toward God or toward earthly power, gain, and materialism.
Jiang says turning desire toward worldly power makes God shine less brightly in a person's life because the soul has chosen to turn away from God.
The canto's account of righteous spirits who pursued honor and fame is glossed by Jiang as a warning that earthly ends weaken the ascent of true love toward heaven.
Jiang says Romeo functions like Dante: a man who did good in political life, was repaid with suspicion and exile, and receives his true reward in heaven.
Jiang says Jesus teaches that worldly wealth is false wealth and that true wealth exists with God.
Jiang frames the moral choice as free will between comfort and wealth on earth with poverty above, or poverty and suffering below with reward above.
Jiang says the next major Dante question is why Jesus had to kill himself, and he previews Beatrice's answer as the most powerful explanation in the poem.
A student proposes that Jesus dies in order to prove he is truly divine to doubters and betrayers.

signature_moments.moment: Free will becomes directional physics: every soul is always aiming its energy somewhere, and the direction itself determines whether God grows brighter or dimmer.
signature_moments.source_phrase: we can choose where to direct our energies
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's clearest compact model of spiritual agency and links politics, desire, and salvation through one mechanism.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang translates Jesus into a brutal economy lesson: the wealth that looks real here is actually poverty, and real wealth may require earthly loss.
signature_moments.source_phrase: all this wealth that we see in this world, it's a false wealth
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the packet's sharp moral reversal and keeps Romeo's story from collapsing into generic piety.

signature_moments.moment: Romeo is made into Dante's double: political service, public suspicion, exile, poverty, and finally heavenly vindication.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows Jiang reading the canto as an encoded autobiography of righteous worldly defeat.

signature_moments.moment: After all the empire history, the lecture snaps back to the scandal that still bothers Dante: why did Jesus have to kill himself at all?
signature_moments.source_phrase: why Jesus had to kill himself again
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It marks the packet's pivot from political-moral order into the poem's deepest atonement puzzle.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The righteous political servant in canto six whom Jiang reads as a Dante parallel: exiled, impoverished, and ultimately rewarded in heaven.
Jiang's phrase for earthly prosperity when measured against the true wealth that exists with God.
The power Jiang says lets human beings direct their energies either toward God and heavenly reward or toward worldly power and loss.

chronology_notes.note: Jiang closes the circa-1300 Florence discussion, extracts a timeless free-will lesson from Justinian's heaven, then uses Romeo to pivot into the next canto's question about Christ's sacrifice.
